subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 24-year-old woman from rural Brazil presents with 2 months of intermittent bloody stools, abdominal pain, and fatigue. She reports swimming most days in a freshwater river near her home. Examination shows mild hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, a low mean corpuscular volume, and eosinophilia. Stool microscopy shows eggs with a lateral spine.
question: Which of the following is the most likely route by which this patient was infected?

options.text: Larval penetration of skin from sandy soil
Ingestion of cysts in untreated water
Ingestion of larvae in raw freshwater fish
A tick bite after exposure in wooded areas
Cercariae from an intermediate snail host penetrating skin

explanation_correct: Schistosoma mansoni is acquired when cercariae released by a snail intermediate host penetrate the skin of a human in contact with contaminated fresh water, such as someone swimming or bathing in a river. The adult worms live in the mesenteric venules, and S mansoni and S japonicum produce intestinal schistosomiasis with diarrhea, abdominal pain, and iron deficiency anemia, as well as periportal fibrosis, liver and spleen enlargement, and portal hypertension. The lateral-spined egg identifies S mansoni, and treatment is praziquantel.

explanation_incorrect.A: Larval penetration of skin from sandy soil is the route for hookworms, which cause cutaneous larva migrans and blood-loss anemia but not eggs with a lateral spine or portal fibrosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Cysts in untreated water transmit Giardia and Entamoeba, which cause nonbloody fatty diarrhea or bloody dysentery with liver abscess rather than a trematode with a lateral-spined egg.
explanation_incorrect.C: Larvae in raw freshwater fish transmit Diphyllobothrium latum and Clonorchis sinensis, and the Clonorchis picture is biliary disease rather than intestinal and hepatic schistosomiasis.
explanation_incorrect.D: A tick bite after wooded exposure raises Babesia or Borrelia burgdorferi, which cause hemolytic febrile illness or erythema migrans rather than fluke disease.

educationalObjective: Schistosoma cercariae released from a snail intermediate host penetrate intact skin during freshwater contact, causing intestinal disease (S mansoni) or bladder disease (S haematobium).

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 58-year-old man who emigrated from Egypt 20 years ago presents with 3 months of painless gross hematuria. He has no fever or flank pain, and he recalls swimming in irrigation canals as a child. Urinalysis shows many red blood cells without casts or dysmorphic forms. Cystoscopy shows a sessile bladder lesion, and biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma.
question: Which of the following correctly identifies the infecting organism, its egg morphology, and the resulting complication?

options.text: S mansoni, whose eggs have a lateral spine and which causes squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
S haematobium, whose eggs have a lateral spine and which causes portal hypertension
S haematobium, whose eggs have a terminal spine and which causes squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
S japonicum, whose eggs have a lateral spine and which causes painless hematuria
Clonorchis sinensis, whose eggs have an operculum and which causes cholangiocarcinoma

explanation_correct: Chronic infection with Schistosoma haematobium causes squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, presenting with painless hematuria, and First Aid lists hematuria with squamous cell bladder cancer as the hint association; chronic infection can also produce pulmonary hypertension. The diagnostic egg has a terminal spine. In contrast, S mansoni eggs have a lateral spine and cause intestinal disease with periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension, as does S japonicum.

explanation_incorrect.A: S mansoni eggs do have a lateral spine, but that species is linked to intestinal disease and portal hypertension rather than bladder squamous cell carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: S haematobium is the right organism, but its eggs have a terminal spine rather than a lateral spine, and its complication is bladder disease rather than portal hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.D: S japonicum is associated with intestinal disease and portal hypertension, not with painless hematuria and bladder carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Clonorchis sinensis is acquired by eating undercooked fish and causes biliary tract inflammation with pigmented gallstones and cholangiocarcinoma, not bladder squamous cell carcinoma.

educationalObjective: Painless hematuria progressing to squamous cell bladder carcinoma after freshwater exposure indicates chronic Schistosoma haematobium, whose eggs have a terminal spine.
